clue.text: He gives false warning of a Mistral storm

indicators.note: a storm throws things into turmoil, so the letters of the wind's name are churned into a new order

explanation.surface: A forecaster cries wolf about the cold wind that blows down the Rhône valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'storm' is the anagram signal working on MISTRAL, with the A kept at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who raises needless alarms or spreads scare stories is a scaremonger who warns of dangers that are not real.

clue.text: Forgetting his opening words, his brother was terribly cut up

definitions.text: Forgetting his opening words, his brother was terribly cut up

parts.words: Forgetting his opening words, his brother was terribly cut up
parts.note: in the Arabian Nights tale, the hero's brother Cassim forgets the password for opening the cave and is hacked to pieces by the forty thieves

explanation.surface: A man whose brother forgot his lines was deeply upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening words' is the magic password 'open sesame', and 'cut up' means literally hacked apart, not upset.
explanation.definitionFit: The woodcutter of the forty thieves tale had a greedy brother Cassim, who forgot the password and was killed inside the cave.

clue.text: The consequence being one gets out the mower again

definitions.meaning: a result or after-effect, usually of something bad

definitions.text: one gets out the mower again
definitions.meaning: originally the word meant a second crop of grass mown later in the same season

explanation.surface: Someone has to mow the lawn a second time as a result of something.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means an after-effect, and in farming it was the second growth of grass cut after the first hay.

clue.text: Modern theatre Shakespeare may have found refreshing

definitions.meaning: a London theatre at Blackfriars, opened in 1959
a London tavern of that name where Ben Jonson and, by tradition, Shakespeare drank

explanation.surface: A new playhouse that Shakespeare might have enjoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are London places: a theatre founded in 1959 and a tavern in Cheapside said to have hosted Shakespeare and Ben Jonson.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the 1959 London playhouse and the Elizabethan Cheapside tavern took their name from the sea-maiden, half woman and half fish.

clue.text: Auster on a place in Wiltshire

parts.note: Auster is the Latin name for the south wind, so S plus WIND
taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer named Auster visits a town in south-west England.
explanation.walkthrough: Auster looks like a surname (Paul Auster) but is the Roman south wind. Swindon is a railway town in Wiltshire, an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: Swindon is a large town in the English county of Wiltshire.

clue.text: Strip rich man that is bareheaded

parts.note: Dives is the traditional name of the rich man in Jesus's parable of the rich man and Lazarus

indicators.note: bareheaded means with the head uncovered, so the first letter of the word is taken off

parts.note: the pronoun 'that' can be replaced by 'it'

explanation.surface: A wealthy man takes off his hat and starts to undress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bareheaded' takes the first letter off IT, leaving T; 'is' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To divest is to strip someone of clothing, property or rights.

clue.text: Perhaps one's tried at court-martial for this

definitions.text: Perhaps one's tried at court-martial for this

parts.words: Perhaps one's tried at court-martial for this
parts.note: a military court tries soldiers for offences such as leaving their post without leave

explanation.surface: A remark about what offence a soldier faces at a military trial.
explanation.walkthrough: Abandoning one's post or unit is a classic offence tried by court-martial.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaving the armed forces without permission is a serious military offence.

clue.text: Short vacation seen, say, as a prophylactic

parts.note: VAC is the usual short form of vacation, especially a university holiday

indicators.note: say tells us the word seen is to be heard, not spelt, in the answer

parts.note: said aloud, these words sound like CINE

explanation.surface: A brief holiday is regarded as preventive medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: VAC is followed by letters that sound like 'seen', spelt CINE.
explanation.definitionFit: A jab of weakened germs prepares the immune system to prevent disease, so it is a preventive.

clue.text: Trickery sounds trifling

indicators.note: sounds says the answer is said like another word

parts.note: trifling means small or unimportant, as slight does

explanation.surface: Deception that seems insignificant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sounds' signals that the answer is said the same as SLIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleight is skilful deception, as in sleight of hand.

clue.text: Prohibits teetotallers consuming rough cider in the first place

indicators.note: the first place tells us the word in goes at the very front of the answer

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: consuming means eating up, so one piece swallows the other inside it

parts.note: TT, short for teetotal, is a crossword label for someone who does not drink; TTS is the plural

indicators.note: rough means roughly handled or crude, so the letters of cider are knocked out of order

explanation.surface: Non-drinkers ban the strong farmhouse drink from the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rough' is the anagram signal on 'cider', 'consuming' puts that inside the teetotallers, and 'in the first place' sets 'in' at the front. TT (teetotal) is standard crossword shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: Interdicts are formal bans, so the verb means forbids or bans.

clue.text: A character on the staff marks the pitch

definitions.text: A character on the staff marks the pitch

parts.words: A character on the staff marks the pitch
parts.note: staff is the five-line musical stave, and pitch is how high or low the notes sound, not a playing field

explanation.surface: A member of the groundstaff marks out the lines of a sports field.
explanation.walkthrough: The staff and the pitch seem to belong to a cricket or football ground; in music the staff carries the notes and this sign at its start fixes their pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: The treble or bass sign at the start of a musical stave fixes which line stands for which note.

clue.text: World War II warbler

parts.note: a warbler is usually a songbird, but here it is anything that wails, like a wartime siren

explanation.surface: A songbird that sang through the Second World War.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain during World War II a wailing siren warned that bombers were coming.
explanation.definitionFit: The rising and falling siren sounded to tell people to take shelter from bombers.

clue.text: Light polishing work brought him his fortune

definitions.text: Light polishing work brought him his fortune

parts.words: Light polishing work brought him his fortune
parts.note: light polishing reads as a gentle buff, but it is the polishing of a light, a magic lamp whose genie made a poor boy rich

explanation.surface: A man made his fortune from easy jobs buffing things.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Arabian Nights tale, rubbing an old oil lamp summons a genie who grants the hero wealth.
explanation.definitionFit: The hero of the Arabian Nights story rubbed a magic lamp, summoned a genie and won riches and a princess.

clue.text: In a musical flower the ends appear undamaged

parts.note: taken as written
a viola is both a stringed instrument and a garden flower like a pansy

indicators.note: ends asks for the first and last letters of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A blossom in a stage show looks perfect at its tips.
explanation.walkthrough: VIOLA is musical (the instrument) and a flower; 'the ends' gives T and E, the first and last letters of 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inviolate is unharmed, intact and kept from violation.

clue.text: Orders revision of credits

indicators.note: a revision reworks something, so the letters of credits are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A film's closing titles are re-edited on instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revision of' signals an anagram of CREDITS.
explanation.definitionFit: To direct people is to instruct or command them, so the verb means instructs.

clue.text: Going the pace like Chaucer's pilgrims

definitions.text: Going the pace like Chaucer's pilgrims

parts.words: Going the pace like Chaucer's pilgrims
parts.note: a horse's easy gallop takes its name from the pace of pilgrims riding to Canterbury, as in Chaucer's Tales

explanation.surface: Moving along at the speed of medieval pilgrims.
explanation.walkthrough: The horse's gait is named from the 'Canterbury gallop', the easy pace of pilgrims riding to Canterbury, as in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse's three-beat gait between trot and gallop is named from the easy pace of riders bound for Canterbury.

clue.text: What a Mikado would do to his sublime object

definitions.text: What a Mikado would do to his sublime object

parts.words: What a Mikado would do to his sublime object
parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's opera the Mikado sings that he will reach his 'object all sublime' in time

explanation.surface: A question of how a Japanese emperor treats something lofty he wants.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mikado's song in Gilbert and Sullivan's opera begins 'My object all sublime / I shall ___ in time'.
explanation.definitionFit: To reach a goal is to attain or accomplish it, which is what the emperor sings he will do.

clue.text: A capital mount for St John

definitions.text: A capital mount for St John

parts.words: A capital mount for St John
parts.note: capital means of the head: John the Baptist's head was brought to Salome on a large dish, and the word also means a warhorse, a mount

explanation.surface: An excellent horse for a saint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' reads as excellent but means 'for a head': John the Baptist's head was presented on a large platter. The word also means a cavalry horse, a mount.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a large flat dish, like the one bearing the Baptist's head, and a warhorse.

clue.text: Wicked to give one military award by word of mouth

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
MM is the Military Medal, a British gallantry award
oral means spoken rather than written

explanation.surface: A complaint that handing out medals by speech alone is sinful.
explanation.walkthrough: MM is the Military Medal, a British army decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: Immoral behaviour breaks moral rules and so is wrong or sinful.

clue.text: Concentrated in the future perhaps

parts.note: taken as written
the future is one example of a grammatical tense, hence 'perhaps'

explanation.surface: Someone imagines the focused mind of things to come.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the future' looks like time to come, but in grammar it is a tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Intense effort or feeling is concentrated, strong and focused.

clue.text: Less than one dozen, about fifty-one (how one does adore figures!)

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is placed round another
less than means a bit short, so the final letter of the word dozen is dropped

parts.note: a dozen is twelve; the word itself is used
LI is fifty-one in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Fewer than twelve, around fifty-one: an exclamation about loving numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Less than' trims 'dozen' to DOZE, and 'about' wraps that round the Roman numeral, giving DOLIZE. The figures adored are idols, not numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: To revere images or worship idols is to make idols of them, hence to worship.

clue.text: Highest quality pig-food on a sailing ship

parts.note: top means best or of the highest quality
mast is the nuts, such as acorns and beechnuts, on which pigs were fed

explanation.surface: First-rate swill for pigs carried on board a sailing vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: MAST is the fallen nuts of forest trees, on which pigs were fattened. The definition is loose: it names where the answer is found.
explanation.definitionFit: A topmast is the section of mast fixed above the lower mast on a sailing vessel.

clue.text: Ancient Jews, coming up to look round the cape

indicators.note: in a down entry coming up means read from the bottom upwards, so the letters run backwards
round means surrounding, so one piece goes about another

parts.note: to look is to see
ness is a word for a cape or headland, common in Scottish place names

explanation.surface: Old Hebrews come forward to inspect what lies around the headland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' makes SENESSE, which 'coming up' turns backwards in this down entry. The Essenes were a Jewish sect of Roman times.
explanation.definitionFit: The Essenes were an ascetic Jewish sect of the Second Temple period, linked with the Dead Sea Scrolls.

clue.text: In which we visit dreamland

parts.note: the god of dreams in Greek myth holds sleepers in his embrace

explanation.surface: A description of a place where we travel in sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: Morpheus is the Greek god of dreams; to be in his embrace is to be asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Being held by the god of dreams is the stock phrase for being fast asleep.

clue.text: Prince implying that you on the other hand go left ?

parts.words: implying that you on the other hand go left
parts.note: the speaker states his own direction, the opposite of the listener's, and the prince's name split into a pronoun, a verb and a direction letter says it

explanation.surface: A prince hints that the other person should take the left turn.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the name into a pronoun, a verb and an abbreviation for a direction, and it says the speaker turns right, so the other person goes left. Prince Igor is Borodin's opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Igor is the Russian hero of Borodin's opera, the twelfth-century prince of Novgorod-Seversky.

clue.text: Whereby Edward once lost five bob ?

definitions.text: Whereby Edward once lost five bob

parts.words: Whereby Edward once lost five bob
parts.note: a crown was an old British coin worth five shillings (five bob), and Edward VIII gave up the Crown in 1936

explanation.surface: A tale of a man called Edward losing five shillings.
explanation.walkthrough: A crown was a British coin worth five shillings ('bob' is slang for a shilling); Edward VIII gave up his crown in 1936.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving up the throne is renouncing the crown, as Edward VIII did in 1936.

clue.text: Madame Grey is without money for salmon

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece is put round the money

parts.note: gris is French for grey; with Madame it takes the feminine form grise
L stands for the pound (libra), British money

explanation.surface: A Frenchwoman called Grey is broke, so she buys a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' here means outside: GRISE goes round L. 'Madame' tells you to use the French feminine. A grilse is a young salmon back from the sea for the first time.
explanation.definitionFit: A grilse is a young salmon that has spent one winter at sea and returned to fresh water.

clue.text: Traces set — gives a lot of trouble

indicators.note: trouble stirs things up, so the letters of set and gives are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that a set of something causes a great deal of bother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a lot of trouble' signals an anagram of SET and GIVES.
explanation.definitionFit: Vestiges are small remaining signs or remnants of something that once existed.
